design_detail: Scoping review (following the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, with JBI scoping-review guidance cited) of US studies published 2013–2022 that quantified misclassification of opioid involvement in drug-overdose deaths: deaths certified with no named drug ('unspecified'), how that share varied by place and by the medicolegal death investigation (MDI) system (coroner or medical examiner, centralized or decentralized), how many unspecified deaths involved opioids, and whether the specific opioid (heroin, fentanyl) was named. PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus were searched in October 2022 with MeSH terms; English and US only; two reviewers screened independently; data were extracted by each reviewer and consolidated into three tables; no risk-of-bias appraisal and no pooling, by design. 17 studies were included, all described as repeated cross-sectional surveillance analyses with data from 1999 to 2019: national analyses of the multiple-cause-of-death files of the National Vital Statistics System (NVSS), one of the CDC State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS, 38 states and Washington DC), one comparing poison-centre and death-certificate data, and state or county record-linkage or case-review studies (Maryland, Florida, Kentucky twice, Marion County Indiana, San Francisco, New York City, Allegheny County Pennsylvania). Read as the PubMed Central author manuscript (NIHMS2046083) of the article published in Annals of Epidemiology.
can_establish: Which US studies published 2013–2022 measured how far death certificates miss or misname opioid involvement, what each reported as the review summarizes it, and the range of those results: national corrections putting opioid-involved deaths about 20–35% above reported counts in 1999–2015, a share of overdose deaths with no named drug that fell from about a quarter around 2008–2010 to 8% in 2018 and differed widely by state, more unspecified certificates where coroners rather than medical examiners certify, and additional opioid-positive or heroin-related deaths found whenever toxicology or scene data were linked.
cannot_establish: The true size of the undercount (no appraisal or pooling, and the national range comes from three analyses by one author with one approach on the same national files); whether opioids caused the additional deaths found by toxicology linkage (several included studies counted an opioid found in post-mortem toxicology); how often deaths are wrongly put down to opioids or to the wrong opioid (the review asks only about underestimation); whether coroner systems cause more unspecified certificates (cross-sectional associations between jurisdictions); or anything about other countries, other drugs, or deaths after 2019.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Database search in October 2022 of PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus, combining MeSH terms for coroners and medical examiners, opioid-related disorders, the opioid epidemic, opiate overdose, drug overdose, death certificates, suicide and cause of death; reference lists of the included studies were checked and added nothing (Methods › 1; Results › 1). The included studies used death certificates in the national multiple-cause-of-death files and records of state or county medical examiners and coroners (toxicology, death-scene notes), with data years from 1999 to 2019.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed studies in English, conducted in the US, published 2013–2022, covering MDI systems, death certificates or overdose surveillance methods. The start year was chosen to cover the rise of synthetic opioid deaths. Excluded: trend descriptions that did not quantify misclassification; descriptions of one data source or method without a quantified comparison with another dataset; work that was not peer-reviewed; studies of risk factors or disparities in drug-related mortality; qualitative studies, commentaries, opinions, case reports and editorials (Methods › 1. Search Strategy and Data Sources).
sample.demographics: By the editors' reading of Tables 1–3: 9 studies used national data (7 the NVSS multiple-cause-of-death files, 1 SUDORS for 38 states and Washington DC, 1 the National Poison Data System against the Drug-Involved Mortality data built from certificate literal text) and 8 used state or county data (Maryland; Florida; Kentucky, two studies; Marion County, Indiana; San Francisco; New York City; Allegheny County, Pennsylvania). Ruhm 2017 appears in both Table 1 and Table 2, so the tables hold 18 rows for 17 studies.
sample.selection_effects: Three databases, English only, US only, a 2013–2022 publication window, no grey literature (so reports of public bodies enter only through journal papers), and search strings given as MeSH headings without the strings used in Web of Science and Scopus; the authors call their terms not exhaustive. Inclusion required a quantified comparison with another source, and the question is framed as underestimation, so the set is built to find missed opioid deaths; no study was sought on deaths wrongly attributed to opioids. Three of the national estimates are by one author (Ruhm 2016, 2017 and 2018) analysing overlapping years of the same national files. Reasons for the 24 full-text exclusions are given only in Figure 1, an image that could not be viewed (screenshot blank).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. In the included studies the 'exposure' is the data source or the certification setting: a death certificate with or without a named drug (multiple-cause ICD-10 coding in the NVSS files), the jurisdiction's MDI system, and linkage with post-mortem toxicology, death-scene investigation notes, prescription-monitoring data or a second register. Opioid involvement among unspecified deaths was estimated in three ways, as the tables describe them: statistical prediction or imputation from deaths with a named drug (Ruhm's three studies), proportional reallocation (Buchanich 2018), and linkage or case review in which an opioid or a heroin marker (6-monoacetylmorphine, a morphine-to-codeine ratio, scene evidence) found at investigation counted the death as opioid- or heroin-involved.
exposure.polysubstance: Not analysed by the review. It does not say how each included study counted deaths with several drugs; the Discussion (4th paragraph) notes that polysubstance and stimulant-involved deaths may pose further documentation problems and calls for studies of their misclassification.

comparison.controls: Within the included studies: counts from death certificates compared with corrected counts (prediction, imputation, reallocation) or with counts after linkage to toxicology, scene investigation or a second register (Florida Medical Examiners Commission data; SUDORS; poison-centre data); coroner jurisdictions compared with medical-examiner jurisdictions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). For the comparisons of MDI systems, the authors name differences in resources for toxicology and scene investigation, training and the timeliness of reports as possible explanations; only Denham et al. (2022), as tabulated, adjusted for individual, county and state characteristics.

outcomes.instruments: An extraction table per study (aim, design, inclusion criteria, exposure, outcome, covariates, analytic method, key findings), filled by each of two reviewers and consolidated (Methods › 2. Review and analysis). No appraisal instrument.
outcomes.validity_norms: Neither the included studies nor the reference sources they used (toxicology panels, scene notes, case review) were appraised; the authors state that a scoping review does not include a risk-of-bias assessment.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Misclassification' means an opioid-involved death certified with no named drug ('unspecified': a certificate on which no specific drug was identified, per the table notes) or a death in which the specific opioid was not named, judged against a correction method or a second source. In several state and county studies a death was counted as opioid- or heroin-involved because the substance or its marker was found in post-mortem toxicology; the review reports these as additional opioid-related or heroin-related deaths.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently and met to resolve discrepancies; each extracted data, then the two compared and consolidated them.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling; figures as the review reports them. National corrections: Ruhm 2018, corrected counts 21–35% above reported counts for any opioid and 20–35% for heroin or synthetic opioids across 1999–2015, corrected rates 12.5 and 7.4 per 100,000 against reported 10.3 and 6.2; Ruhm 2017, corrected opioid-involved rates 24% and heroin rates 22% above reported rates in 2014; Buchanich 2018, about 72% of unspecified unintentional overdose deaths in 1999–2015 estimated opioid-related, about 70,000 deaths reallocated. Share of overdose deaths with no named drug: about 25% in 2008–2010, 15–20% in 2014–2016, 8% in 2018; from 0% (Washington DC) to 63.8% (Louisiana) in 2008. Coroner against medical-examiner counties (Denham 2022): odds of an unclassified overdose death OR 1.77 (95% CI 1.08 to 2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32 to 6.46) in 2018. Linkage: Florida 8,633 more opioid-related deaths (34% of the NVSS count, 2003–2017); Maryland 1,052 more heroin-related deaths (given as 26% of all drug-related overdose deaths, 2012–2015); Marion County 86.8% of unspecified deaths opioid-positive, opioid-involved share from 34.2% to 86.0% (642 more cases); Kentucky 44 more potentially heroin-related deaths (2%) in 2013–2014, and in 2015 4.7% heroin-positive deaths certified as unspecified and 6% more fentanyl-positive deaths; heroin deaths up 21% in San Francisco (text), 17% in New York City, and from 171 to 245 in Allegheny County.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Covariates of the included studies are listed in the tables: individual, county and state characteristics in Denham 2022 and in Ruhm's models; 'not applicable' or 'not listed' for most linkage studies.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The review states that it followed PRISMA-ScR.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's national figure rests on one author's three analyses and is stated as an underestimate of 20–35% (see interpretation gap). Additional deaths found by toxicology linkage are reported as opioid- or heroin-related without separating presence from cause. The overcounting direction appears in one sentence of the Discussion, and the reclassifications that lowered counts attributed to morphine and codeine (Allegheny County) are reported only as heroin gains.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Seventeen unappraised US studies with data from 1999 to 2019, all repeated cross-sectional analyses of death records. Three national analyses by one author put corrected opioid-involved counts 20–35% above reported counts across 1999–2015 (24% in 2014); a fourth reallocated about 72% of unspecified unintentional deaths as opioid-related by assuming they matched specified deaths. The share of overdose deaths with no named drug fell from about a quarter around 2008–2010 to 8% in 2018 and ranged from 0% to 63.8% between states in 2008. Three studies found more unspecified certificates in coroner than in medical-examiner jurisdictions (in one, adjusted OR 1.77 in 2014 and 3.87 in 2018). Every state or county linkage study found additional deaths with an opioid or heroin marker, or reclassified deaths to heroin, when toxicology or scene data were added.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says opioid involvement "was underestimated nationally by 20–35%" (Abstract › Results; the Conclusion says "by as much 20–35%"). Gaps: (1) corrected counts 20–35% above reported counts mean reported counts were about 17–26% below the corrected ones (editors' calculation: 1 − 1/1.20 and 1 − 1/1.35), and the range is one author's year-by-year estimates under one model, not agreement among independent studies; (2) the Results say coroner counties were four times more likely to record an unspecified death, which restates one study's 2018 odds ratio of 3.87 as a likelihood (the 2014 odds ratio was 1.77) when 8–19% of deaths were unspecified, so the ratio of probabilities would be smaller; (3) deaths found by toxicology linkage are called opioid-related or heroin-related although several studies counted an opioid found, a limitation the Discussion itself states (drug screening can mark a death as drug-involved when the drug did not contribute, 5th paragraph); (4) the recommendations to train coroners, change their qualifications and add resources rest on cross-sectional associations between jurisdictions, and the suggestion that elected coroners may hesitate to certify opioid deaths for fear of consequences for constituents' families is not examined by any included study; (5) against this, the scoping design and the absence of appraisal are stated plainly, and the limitations name the language, database and date limits; (6) the Discussion calls the national 20–35% consistent with studies at the state level (refs 40 and 41), but Horon's 26% is additional heroin-related deaths as a share of all overdose deaths, not a rise over a reported heroin count, and Quast's 34% compares Florida's medical-examiner records with the national files for Florida; neither is a model correction like Ruhm's, so the agreement is between different measures.

timeline.event: Warner et al. (Academic Forensic Pathology): state differences in completeness of manner and drug specification on certificates, 2008–2010; included in this review (Table 1).
Ruhm (Population Health Metrics): statistical adjustment of drug-poisoning deaths, 1999–2012; included (Table 2).
Ruhm (American Journal of Preventive Medicine): corrected state opioid and heroin mortality rates, 2008–2014; included (Tables 1 and 2).
Ruhm (Addiction): corrected national opioid-involved deaths, 1999–2015; source of the 20–35% range; included (Table 2)
Buchanich et al.: unspecified unintentional overdose deaths reallocated, 1999–2015; included (Table 2; card sc_buchanich_2018)
Horon et al.: enhanced surveillance against standard certificates for heroin deaths, Maryland 2012–2015; included (Table 2; card sc_horon_2018)
Denham et al.: coroner county systems associated with higher odds of unclassified overdose deaths, 2014 and 2018; included (Table 1).

Drake and Ruhm (American Journal of Preventive Medicine), cited in the Introduction and Discussion: almost 6% of overdose deaths listed no specific drug category in 2020; published after the search and not an included study.
This review (online December 2024): by its authors' account the first synthesis of the literature on misclassification of fatal opioid overdose.

replication.where_it_stands: The only review of opioid misclassification in US death data that its authors know of. Its national figure rests on Ruhm's three analyses, which share author, data and approach, so the 20–35% range is one estimate repeated, not replication. Buchanich 2018 and Horon 2018, also read for this round, are inside it: claims must not cite the review and those studies as independent support. Deaths after 2019, other countries, stimulants and the overcounting direction are outside its scope.

funding.declared_conflicts: Acknowledgments: Deborah S. Hasin reports a relationship with Syneos Health that includes funding grants; the other authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships. The Declaration of interests in the footnotes states that the authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors are at Columbia University (Department of Epidemiology, Mailman School of Public Health; one also in the Department of Emergency Medicine), one also at the New York State Psychiatric Institute. No review author appears among the named authors of the included studies in the reference list (some entries end in et al.).

what_would_settle_it: A national validation study that samples drug-poisoning deaths at random across coroner and medical-examiner jurisdictions, certified with and without a named drug, re-investigates each with full quantitative toxicology, scene and history review by forensic pathologists blind to the certificate and using one standard case definition, and reports both how many opioid-caused deaths the certificates missed or misnamed and how many certified opioid deaths the review would not attribute to opioids.

domains.note: Three databases, dates, explicit criteria, duplicate independent screening and PRISMA-ScR reporting; but English and US only, no grey literature, search strings given only as MeSH headings, a 2013–2022 window, and exclusion reasons only in an image that could not be viewed.
No appraisal of the included studies or of their reference sources, by design; toxicology presence, scene review and statistical prediction are reported side by side as findings of misclassification.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 17 included studies is by the review's authors, as far as the reference list shows.

The Results report the studies' figures, with the citation and number errors listed under reporting issues; the Discussion and Conclusion add recommendations (coroner training and qualifications, resources) and an explanation (elected coroners' hesitation) that no included study tested.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on undercounting against overcounting (overcounting under-represented)
domains.note: The question, search and synthesis concern underestimation only; deaths wrongly put down to opioids appear in one Discussion sentence, and reclassifications that lowered morphine and codeine counts are reported only as heroin gains.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a scoping review (METHODS §5.3), and it is not rated as a systematic review. It maps the US literature transparently and says it does not appraise, but its figures are unappraised second-hand summaries, its national range comes from one author's repeated analyses, and its frame looks only for missed opioid deaths. Citable for: which US studies measured opioid misclassification in 2013–2022 and what they reported, as pointers to the primary studies (whose own figures should be cited from their full texts); the fall in unspecified certificates to 8% by 2018 and the state range in 2008, as second-hand figures; the association of coroner systems with more unspecified certificates in three studies. Not citable for: a national undercount of 20–35% as an established fact, causation of the additional deaths found by toxicology, the effect of coroner training, or the overcounting direction.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus searched in October 2022 for US studies in English published 2013–2022; 117 records after duplicates, 76 excluded at title and abstract, 24 at full text, 17 included; reference lists of included studies added none; no risk-of-bias assessment because the review is a scoping review.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 1. Search Strategy and Data Sources, 1st paragraph; Methods › 2. Review and analysis, 1st paragraph; Results › 1. Sample and Study Characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Exclusion reasons are only in Figure 1 (PRISMA diagram), an image: figure image not viewable. The Discussion (6th paragraph) says removing duplicates eliminated 66% of all imported records, which would put the records imported at about 340 to 350 (editors' calculation from the 117 left); only Figure 1 could confirm it.

key_findings.finding: The share of overdose deaths with no specific drug on the certificate fell from about 25% in 2008–2010 to 15–20% in 2014–2016 and 8% in 2018. Per Table 1: 19.3% in 2014 and 8% in 2018 (Denham 2022); 25.4% in 2008 and 19.5% in 2014 (Ruhm 2017); 24.4% in 2010 to 14.6% in 2016, 20.3% overall (Tote 2019).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2. Misclassification of Cause of Death, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: The share of unspecified overdose deaths ranged from 0% in Washington DC to 63.8% in Louisiana in 2008; South Carolina fell from 39.8% (2008) to 6.0% (2014), a drop of 33.8 percentage points; Southern states had higher shares than the Northeast and West (Ruhm 2017).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.1 Geographic Variation in Unspecified Drug-related Overdose Deaths, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Three studies found lower shares of unspecified overdose deaths where medical examiners rather than coroners certify, and centralized medical-examiner systems lower than decentralized ones. In Denham 2022, coroner systems had higher odds of an unclassified overdose death, OR 1.77 (1.08 to 2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32 to 6.46) in 2018; unclassified deaths fell by 72% in medical-examiner counties and 43% in coroner counties between 2014 and 2018; odds were lower where the certifier is a pathologist, violent deaths are investigated, coroners must be trained, or the system is centralized.
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.1.1 Variation by Medicolegal Death Investigation (MDI) System, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Denham et al. 2022 row)
key_findings.note: The text's 'four times more likely' restates the 2018 odds ratio; these are cross-sectional associations between jurisdictions.

key_findings.finding: National corrections from NVSS data: corrected counts 21–35% above reported counts for any opioid and 20–35% for heroin or synthetic opioids, 1999–2015, with corrected rates of 12.5 and 7.4 per 100,000 against reported 10.3 and 6.2, and 23.1% of overdose deaths with no drug specified (26% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015) (Ruhm 2018); corrected opioid-involved rates 24% and heroin rates 22% above reported rates in 2014 (Ruhm 2017).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.2.1 Misclassification of opioid involvement at the national level, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Ruhm C 2018 and Ruhm C 2017 rows)
key_findings.note: All three national prediction or imputation studies are by one author on the same national files; the year of the corrected rates is not given in the table.

key_findings.finding: Buchanich 2018: assuming unspecified unintentional overdose deaths involve opioids in the same proportion as specified ones, about 72% of unspecified deaths in 1999–2015 were estimated opioid-related; about 70,000 deaths were reallocated, the review's table adds 'over 50% in 5 states' without saying whether counts or rates rose, and state rankings changed for all but 8 states.
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.2.1, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Buchanich et al. 2018 row)
key_findings.note: Checked against the primary paper (card sc_buchanich_2018): it reports more than 70,000 reallocated of 97,159 unspecified deaths and does not print 72%, which is that ratio; its rate increases above 50% in 5 states are for 2015, and its counts more than doubled in the same five states over 1999–2015.

key_findings.finding: State and county linkage: Florida local records found 8,633 more opioid-related deaths than the NVSS files (34% of the NVSS count, 2003–2017; Quast 2020); Maryland enhanced surveillance found 1,052 more heroin-related deaths (given as 26% of all drug-related overdose deaths, 2012–2015; Horon 2018); in Marion County, Indiana, 86.8% of unspecified deaths were opioid-positive and adding toxicology raised the opioid-involved share from 34.2% to 86.0% (642 more cases; Lowder 2018).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.2.2 Misclassification of opioid involvement at the state and county level, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Quast, Horon, Lowder rows)
key_findings.note: Checked against the primary paper (card sc_horon_2018): 1,052 of 3,957 overdose deaths is 26.6%, the overdose total is not defined there, and the additional deaths met a broader definition that partly counts heroin markers present in toxicology. Lowder's 642 added cases were recoded because an opioid was found in toxicology, and the table's 'doubled' is a 2.5-fold rise (reporting issue 9).

key_findings.finding: Kentucky: in 2013–2014 a quarter of overdose certificates named no drug although 89% of those deaths had post-mortem toxicology, and 44 more deaths (2%) were classed as potentially heroin-related by morphine-to-codeine ratio; in 2015, 88% had toxicology, 4.7% of overdose deaths were heroin-positive but certified as unspecified, 2.3% more were heroin-positive with heroin not listed, and 6% more were fentanyl-positive (58% of these had no drug listed, 42% other drugs).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.2.2, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Slavova et al. 2017 rows, refs 44 and 45)

key_findings.finding: Specific opioids, national (O'Donnell 2022, SUDORS, 38 states and Washington DC, 2018–2019): 44.2% of probable and 52.6% of suspected heroin deaths listed only morphine on the certificate, and reclassification raised the share of heroin deaths from 80.2% to 93.3%; fentanyl was detected in 73.6% of deaths, and 1% was likely pharmaceutical fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.3.1 Misclassification of heroin- and fentanyl-involvement at the national level, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (O'Donnell et al. 2022 row)
key_findings.note: The share of fentanyl deaths classed as illicitly manufactured fentanyl is 37.1% in the text and 89.3% in Table 3 (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Specific opioids, county studies: in Allegheny County 2008–2010, 66% of 112 unintentional deaths with morphine but not heroin listed met criteria for heroin, and after review heroin deaths rose from 171 to 245 while morphine deaths fell from 132 to 41 and codeine deaths from 34 to 5 (Mertz 2014); in New York City 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication (71%) were attributed to heroin, raising heroin deaths by 17% (Gill 2016); in San Francisco an expanded definition added 20 heroin deaths to 152 (Hurstak).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.3.2 Misclassification of heroin-involvement at the state and county level, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (Mertz, Gill, Hurstak rows)
key_findings.note: The text gives the San Francisco increase as 21%; 20 on 152 is 13% (reporting issue 4). The New York City 17% rise cannot be checked from the review, which gives no base count of heroin deaths.

key_findings.finding: Poison-centre against death-certificate data, 2010–2015 (Mallama 2019): the death-certificate-based Drug-Involved Mortality data held 61 deaths for each one in the National Poison Data System (the table says drug-related overdose deaths; the study's aim concerns opioid-involved fatal cases); multi-substance cases were 77% in the poison-centre data against 58.6%, and suicide 54% against 10% for commonly dispensed opioids.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (Mallama et al. 2019 row); Results › 2.3.1, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Discussion states the opposite direction once: drug screening can mark a death as drug-involved when the person used the drug before death but it did not contribute, and incomplete scene notes can wrongly mark a death as not drug-involved; it endorses autopsy, scene investigation, prescription-monitoring checks and quantitative toxicology, as recommended by the National Association of Medical Examiners and a SAMHSA expert panel.

Limitations stated by the authors: English only, three databases, no grey literature, search terms not exhaustive, included data only through 2019, and possible COVID-19 reporting lags from 2020; the authors suggest content saturation because reference lists added no studies.

Recommendations: more resources for toxicology and scene investigation, training or changed qualifications for coroners, and data integration; the Discussion notes CDC's SUDORS was funded in 12 states in 2016 and 47 states and Washington DC by 2019, and that heroin deaths may still have been underestimated within it in 2018–2019.

reporting_issues.issue: Results › 2, 1st paragraph cites refs 40 and 41 (Maryland and Florida studies) among the nine national studies and omits refs 38 and 39 (the SUDORS and poison-centre studies); the same paragraph lists 40 and 41 again among the eight state or county studies. By the tables, the national studies are refs 17 and 32–39 and the state or county studies refs 31 and 40–46.
reporting_issues.consequence: The counts (9 and 8) are right, but the printed citations cannot be used to tell which studies are national; Horon 2018 is a Maryland study, not a national one.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref 47 (Robinson, 'County coroners and their role in the heart of the opioid epidemic', per the reference list) is cited as if it were an included study in Results › 2, 1st paragraph (31,40–47), Results › 2.2.2 (31,44–47) and Discussion, 1st paragraph (40,41,44–47); the 17 included studies are refs 17 and 31–46.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader may count a piece outside the included set among the evidence for the state and county findings; the findings themselves come from refs 31 and 40–46.

reporting_issues.issue: For O'Donnell 2022, the text says 37.1% of fentanyl deaths were probable or suspected illicitly manufactured fentanyl, while Table 3 gives 89.3%, with 1% pharmaceutical and 9.7% unknown (summing to 100%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.3.1, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (O'Donnell et al. 2022 row)
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither figure should be cited from this review; the primary paper is needed.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says including toxicology reports and case narratives increased the number of heroin deaths identified in San Francisco by 21%, while Table 3 gives 152 deaths by the standard definition and 20 more by the expanded one, an increase of 13% (editors' calculation, 20/152).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.3.2, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (Hurstak et al. row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The 21% cannot be reproduced from the review's own table; check Hurstak et al. (2018) before citing either figure.

reporting_issues.issue: For Kentucky 2015, the text says an additional 4.7% and 6% 'of unspecified deaths' involved heroin and fentanyl; Table 2 gives 4.7% of overdose deaths (heroin-positive but unspecified) and says 42% of the 6% additional fentanyl-positive deaths had other drugs listed, so they were not unspecified.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.2.2, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Slavova et al. 2017, ref 45 row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator is all overdose deaths, not unspecified deaths, and the figures are toxicology-positive deaths, not deaths certified as caused by heroin or fentanyl.

reporting_issues.issue: Results › 2.2.1 says three studies (refs 33, 36, 37) used multiple imputation; Table 2 describes Ruhm 2016 and Ruhm 2018 as predictions from probit models fitted to deaths with a named drug, and only Ruhm 2017 as multiple imputation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.2.1, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Ruhm rows)
reporting_issues.consequence: A labelling inconsistency; all three approaches assume that unspecified deaths resemble specified deaths with the same recorded characteristics, an assumption the review does not discuss.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations paragraph describes checking the reference lists of the included studies as a 'forward search'; reference-list checking is backward searching, and no search of later citing papers is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of likely content saturation rests on backward checking only.

reporting_issues.issue: The Acknowledgments report a relationship between one author (Hasin) and Syneos Health that includes funding grants, while the Declaration of interests in the footnotes says the authors have no known competing interests.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Acknowledgments; Footnotes › Declaration of interests
reporting_issues.consequence: Both statements are recorded; the disclosed relationship is not about death certification.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 (Lowder et al. row) says including toxicology results 'doubled' the share of opioid-involved deaths from 34.2% to 86.0%; that is about a 2.5-fold rise (editors' calculation, 86.0/34.2 = 2.51). The same row says unspecified and other cases were recoded as opioid-involved because an opioid was found in the toxicology report.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 (Lowder et al. 2018 row)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the two percentages, not 'doubled'; the 642 added cases had an opioid present at death, which does not show that it caused the death.

reporting_issues.issue: Results › 2 says the state and county studies covered seven states across the Northeast, South and West; by Tables 2 and 3 the seven are California, Florida, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, New York and Pennsylvania, and Indiana (Marion County) is in the Midwest.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2. Misclassification of Cause of Death, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; describe the state and county studies by state, or as covering four regions.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation and spelling errors: Hurstak et al. is dated 2017 in Table 3 and 2018 in the reference list (reference 31); 'Statitistics' (reference 3); SAMHSA is called the 'Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Association' (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
